summary.text: An ion is an atom or molecule with a net electrical charge, because its electrons and protons are not equal in number.
An atom with more electrons than protons is a negative anion, and one with fewer electrons than protons is a positive cation.
Opposite charges attract, so cations and anions readily pair up to form ionic compounds, and they can be freed into solution when a salt dissolves.

facts.label: Net charge rule
facts.value: Protons minus electrons gives an ion's charge

facts.label: Who named it
facts.value: Michael Faraday introduced the term ion in 1834

facts.label: Size change
facts.value: Anions are larger than the parent atom; cations are smaller

facts.label: Where seen
facts.value: Seawater holds ions from dissolved salts

facts.label: Single-atom ions
facts.value: Called monatomic; two or more atoms make a polyatomic ion

items.prompt: An atom ends up with 11 protons but only 10 electrons. What is it?

options.label: A neutral atom, since the numbers are close to equal
A positively charged cation
A negatively charged anion
A zwitterion with charges spread inside it

items.explain: An ion with fewer electrons than protons has a net positive charge, which makes it a cation.

items.prompt: Two ions drift near each other in water, one positive and one negative. What do you expect?

options.label: They repel each other and drift apart
They ignore each other, as charge only matters in metals
They attract each other and can form an ionic compound
They merge into one neutral atom by trading protons

items.explain: Opposite electric charges are pulled together by electrostatic force, so cations and anions attract and readily form ionic compounds.

items.prompt: A chlorine atom takes on one extra electron. How does its size change?

options.label: It shrinks, because the electron cloud is tighter
It stays the same, since electrons have almost no mass
It loses its electron cloud entirely and becomes a bare nucleus
It grows, because extra electrons repel each other

items.explain: Anions are larger than the parent atom, since the excess electrons repel each other and add to the size of the electron cloud.

items.prompt: A seashell soaks in seawater and you notice the water carries charged particles. Where did they most plausibly come from?

options.label: Dissolved salts that released their ions into the water
Water molecules that split into single protons
Air bubbles that carry a built-in charge
The shell's metal atoms losing all their protons

items.explain: Ions are released into solution when a salt dissolves in a solvent like water, and seawater's ions come from dissolved salts.

items.prompt: Which of these is an ion made of more than one atom?

options.label: Na⁺, the sodium ion
OH⁻, the hydroxide ion
F⁻, the fluoride ion
K⁺, the potassium ion

items.explain: Hydroxide is a polyatomic ion; the others are single-atom ions.

items.prompt: A charged particle moves through a field. Which of these would a physicist expect for an ion?

options.label: Its path bends in electric and magnetic fields
Its path never changes, since atoms are neutral
It is pulled toward a like charge on a plate
It stops moving as soon as it is in solution

items.explain: Ions are attracted to opposite charges and repelled by like charges, and their trajectories can be deflected by magnetic and electric fields.

paragraphs.heading: A charged atom or molecule
paragraphs.text: An ion is an atom or a molecule that carries an overall electric charge. By convention an electron's charge is negative and a proton's is positive, and the two are equal in size but opposite. In an ion the number of electrons does not match the number of protons, so the charges do not cancel out. Its net charge, counted in units of elementary charge, is simply its protons minus its electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Cations and anions
paragraphs.text: A cation has fewer electrons than protons, so it is positive; the potassium ion K⁺ is one. An anion has more electrons than protons, so it is negative, like the chloride ion Cl⁻ or the hydroxide ion OH⁻. Opposite charges pull toward each other by electrostatic force. That is why cations and anions attract and readily join to form ionic compounds.

paragraphs.heading: How ions are written
paragraphs.text: An ion made of a single atom is called monatomic, while one made of two or more atoms is called polyatomic. Its charge is shown as a superscript on the right. A charge of one needs only a plus or minus sign, as in Na⁺ and F⁻. Bigger charges also show the number of extra or missing electrons, as in the peroxide ion O₂²⁻ or He²⁺, which is an alpha particle.

paragraphs.heading: Bigger and smaller
paragraphs.text: Electrons set the size of atoms and molecules. So an anion is larger than the atom or molecule it came from, because its extra electrons repel one another and swell its electron cloud. A cation is smaller than its parent, since its electron cloud is smaller. The hydrogen cation is the extreme case: it has no electrons at all, only a single proton, far smaller than a hydrogen atom.

paragraphs.heading: Where the names come from
paragraphs.text: The word ion comes from a Greek word meaning "to go". Michael Faraday introduced it in 1834, on a suggestion from William Whewell, for the unknown things that travel through a watery solution from one electrode to the other. A cation is something that moves down and an anion something that moves up. The names fit because ions move toward the electrode with the opposite charge.

paragraphs.heading: Salt in water
paragraphs.text: In his 1884 dissertation, Svante Arrhenius explained why solid crystalline salts split into pairs of charged particles when they dissolve. He proposed that free ions form even without an electric current, and this work later won him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. When salts meet a solvent such as water, the freed ions gather a shell of the liquid around themselves. Seawater is an everyday example, holding ions that come from dissolved salts.
